texts.notes: All 24 nutriment statements are present, with the right objects, attention type and polarity. Citation precision: every nutriment claim cites x.2-x.3 but not x.4, which is where the predicate 'ayam āhāro / anāhāro ... fuels/starves' is actually stated. So the left-out note's description of x.4 as a mere restatement is slightly off, since x.4 completes the sentence. Pali nuance for n-18 to n-24: amanasikārabahulīkāro means 'frequent non-attention', or making much of not attending, rather than 'not frequently attending'. The attention field copies the English. The difference is small but worth fixing in the controlled vocabulary. The model also collapses the asymmetric effects ('increase and growth' for the hindrances, 'full development' for the factors) into fuels/starves. That is an acceptable simplification.

omissions.what: A mendicant with good friends can expect to develop and cultivate the seven awakening factors (kalyāṇamittassetaṁ ... pāṭikaṅkhaṁ ... bhāvessati, bahulīkarissati). The Pali gives this in full; it is untranslated, not abbreviated.

How one with good friends develops them: the stock formula, in which each factor relies on seclusion, fading away and cessation and ripens as letting go. The Pali gives it in full apart from an internal …pe… between mindfulness and equanimity. It is not cited for c-17/c-18/c-19/o-19, although the same passage is cited in sn46.12.

texts.notes: The modellers say the rest of the sutta is 'abbreviated in the source'. That is true only of Sujato's English (1.1 ends with '…'). The Pali has 1.2-1.6 in full. 'Fully encoded' with 'nothing' left out is therefore wrong: the text matches sn46.12 1.3-2.4, which they did encode there.

1.6-1.7 vivekanissitaṁ: the factors rely on seclusion. 'Seclusion is the basis of' is a fair converse.
1.6-1.7 virāganissitaṁ: the factors rely on fading away.
1.6-1.7 nirodhanissitaṁ: the factors rely on cessation.
1.5 and 1.11: bodhāya saṁvattanti, 'they lead to awakening', which is why they are called bojjhaṅgā.
1.7 vossaggapariṇāmiṁ, 'ripens as letting go'. 'Leads to letting go' is an acceptable simplification of 'culminates in'.
